questions.question: What is Amazon CloudFront and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: CloudFront is AWS's Content Delivery Network (CDN) service. It solves two problems: (1) High latency — content stored in one region is slow for global users. CloudFront caches it at 600+ edge locations worldwide so users always get content from a nearby server. (2) Security — it allows you to keep your S3 bucket completely private while still serving content publicly, using Origin Access Control (OAC).

questions.question: What is an edge location? How is it different from an AWS Region or Availability Zone?
questions.answer: An edge location is a geographically distributed mini data center used by CloudFront to cache content close to end users. Unlike Regions (large clusters of data centers) and AZs (isolated failure zones within a Region), edge locations exist specifically for caching and delivery — they are not used to run EC2 instances or other compute workloads. CloudFront has 600+ edge locations globally, far more than the ~30 AWS Regions.

questions.question: What is OAC (Origin Access Control) in CloudFront, and why is it used?
questions.answer: OAC is a mechanism that restricts S3 bucket access so that only a specific CloudFront distribution can read from it. You attach OAC to a CloudFront distribution, then update the S3 bucket policy with a condition that allows s3:GetObject only from that distribution's ARN. The S3 bucket remains completely private — direct S3 URLs return 403 Forbidden. OAC is the recommended replacement for the older OAI (Origin Access Identity).

questions.question: What is Route 53? Why is it named Route 53?
questions.answer: Route 53 is AWS's highly available and scalable Domain Name System (DNS) service. It translates human-readable domain names (like www.myshop.com) into IP addresses that computers use. It is named after port 53, which is the standard network port used for DNS communication.

questions.question: What is a hosted zone in Route 53?
questions.answer: A hosted zone is a container in Route 53 that holds all DNS records for a specific domain (e.g., myshop.com) and its subdomains. A public hosted zone routes traffic over the internet. A private hosted zone routes traffic within an Amazon VPC. When you create a hosted zone, Route 53 assigns four name servers to it. You must update your domain registrar to use these name servers so Route 53 becomes authoritative for your domain.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Alias record and a CNAME record in Route 53?
questions.answer: An Alias record is AWS-specific. It maps a domain to an AWS resource (CloudFront, ELB, S3, etc.) using that resource's DNS name. Key advantages: (1) Works at the apex (root) domain like myshop.com, which a CNAME cannot. (2) Queries to AWS resource targets are free. A CNAME record is a standard DNS record that maps one domain name to another, but it cannot be used at the apex domain, and queries are charged.

questions.question: What is the AWS SDK? Name the Python SDK and how to install it.
questions.answer: The AWS SDK (Software Development Kit) is a set of language-specific libraries and tools that let developers interact with AWS services programmatically from application code. Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. Install it with: pip install boto3. Boto3 supports a Client interface (low-level, mirrors the API) and a Resource interface (higher-level, object-oriented). You must configure credentials using 'aws configure' before running Boto3 scripts locally.

questions.question: Why are AMI IDs region-specific? What error do you get if you use the wrong region's AMI ID?
questions.answer: AMI IDs are region-specific because each region maintains its own copy of the operating system images, and each copy gets a unique ID within that region. If you copy an AMI ID from one region (e.g., us-east-1) and use it in a Boto3 script targeting a different region (e.g., ap-south-1), you will get an 'InvalidAMIID.NotFound' error. Always look up the AMI ID in the AWS Console for the specific region you are deploying to.

questions.question: What is the default TTL for objects cached in CloudFront edge locations?
questions.answer: The default TTL (Time-To-Live) for CloudFront is 24 hours (86,400 seconds). After this period, the cached object is considered stale and CloudFront will re-fetch it from the origin on the next request. You can customize TTL per cache behavior using Cache-Control headers, minimum TTL, and maximum TTL settings. You can also force immediate removal of cached content using cache invalidation.

questions.question: What are the three required inputs when creating a CloudFront distribution for S3?
questions.answer: (1) Origin — the S3 bucket where your content lives. (2) Default Root Object — the file CloudFront serves when the root URL is requested (usually index.html). (3) Permissions — specifically Origin Access Control (OAC), which grants CloudFront permission to read from the private S3 bucket. Once the distribution is created, you must also update the S3 bucket policy with the OAC-generated policy that references the distribution ARN.

questions.question: A user in Sydney loads your website in 50ms today. Tomorrow they report it takes 2 seconds. Your S3 files haven't changed. What could explain this?
questions.answer: (Situation) User had fast load times (cache hit from nearby Sydney edge location). Suddenly slow load time reported. (Task) Diagnose the cause. (Action) Investigated CloudFront cache behavior. Two likely causes: (1) The cached object's TTL expired at the edge location — the next request caused a cache miss, forcing CloudFront to fetch from the S3 origin in a distant region. (2) The edge location evicted the object due to low popularity or cache pressure. (Result) First occurrence after TTL expiry is always slower. Subsequent requests will be fast again once re-cached.

questions.question: A team pushed an updated homepage to S3. Users still see the old version 6 hours later. What should they do?
questions.answer: (Situation) New index.html uploaded to S3 but users see stale cached content from CloudFront edge locations. (Task) Force users to see the updated version immediately. (Action) Create a CloudFront cache invalidation for the path /index.html (or /* for all files). This removes the stale cached copy from all edge locations. Next request to any edge location causes a cache miss and fetches the new version from S3. (Result) Users see the updated page on their next request. Note: First 1,000 invalidation paths per month are free; beyond that there is a per-path charge.

questions.question: A developer ran aws configure on an EC2 instance and hardcoded the access keys. Your security team flagged this. What is the correct approach?
questions.answer: (Situation) Access keys hardcoded or stored in aws config on EC2 — security risk if the instance is compromised or config files are exposed. (Task) Remove hardcoded credentials and use a more secure method. (Action) Detach any hardcoded credentials. Create an IAM role with the minimum required permissions. Attach the IAM role to the EC2 instance. Boto3 automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service (169.254.169.254) — no credentials in code or config files. (Result) Credentials are temporary, automatically rotated, and never stored on disk — fully secure and AWS best practice.

questions.question: A company's website is hosted in S3 (Mumbai). US users complain it loads slowly; EU users say it is fine. What is the likely cause and the solution?
questions.answer: (Situation) Inconsistent global performance — EU users fine, US users slow. (Task) Diagnose and improve US user experience. (Action) Diagnosed cause: S3 bucket is in Mumbai. EU has closer edge locations than US would for a Mumbai origin without CloudFront, but with CloudFront the US edge locations should be serving cached content. If CloudFront is not yet set up, US users are going all the way to Mumbai. Solution: Implement CloudFront with the S3 bucket as origin. US edge locations will cache the content and serve it locally. (Result) US users get sub-100ms load times from nearby edge locations.

questions.question: You need to map the apex domain mycompany.com to a CloudFront distribution in Route 53. Which record type do you use and why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to map root domain to CloudFront — not a subdomain. (Task) Create the correct DNS record. (Action) Create an Alias A record in the Route 53 hosted zone for mycompany.com, targeting the CloudFront distribution. Cannot use CNAME because the DNS standard (RFC 1034) prohibits CNAME at the apex domain — it would conflict with the SOA and NS records required at the root. Alias records are an AWS-specific extension that supports apex mapping. (Result) mycompany.com resolves to CloudFront. Alias queries to CloudFront are also free of charge in Route 53.

questions.question: A Python script using Boto3 fails with 'NoCredentialsError'. How do you troubleshoot this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Boto3 script throwing NoCredentialsError. (Task) Find and fix the credentials issue. (Action) Checked the credentials resolution chain: (1) Environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) — none set. (2) ~/.aws/credentials file — file missing or empty. (3) IAM instance profile — script not running on EC2. Fix: Run 'aws configure' to set up credentials, or set environment variables, or run the script on an EC2 instance with an IAM role attached. (Result) After running aws configure with valid IAM user credentials, script executes successfully.

questions.question: A team is doing A/B testing — they want 90% of traffic to go to the stable version and 10% to the new version. Which Route 53 routing policy do they use?
questions.answer: (Situation) Two versions of an application running simultaneously. Need controlled percentage-based traffic split. (Task) Configure DNS routing to achieve 90/10 split. (Action) Use Route 53 Weighted routing policy. Create two records for the same domain: one pointing to stable version with weight 90, one pointing to new version with weight 10. Route 53 distributes traffic proportionally. (Result) 90% of users hit the stable version; 10% test the new version. Weights can be adjusted to gradually shift more traffic to the new version (canary deployment pattern).

questions.question: Your company's primary web server is in us-east-1. You want automatic failover to eu-west-1 if the primary goes down. How do you set this up?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need disaster recovery with automatic DNS failover. (Task) Set up active-passive failover using Route 53. (Action) Use Failover routing policy. (1) Create a Route 53 health check that monitors the us-east-1 endpoint. (2) Create an A record for the domain with Failover type 'Primary', pointing to us-east-1, associated with the health check. (3) Create a second A record with Failover type 'Secondary', pointing to eu-west-1 (no health check required). (Result) Route 53 continuously monitors the primary. If the health check fails, Route 53 automatically serves the Secondary record, routing all traffic to eu-west-1 until the primary recovers.

questions.question: A developer wants to write Python code that lists all objects in an S3 bucket and prints their names. Write the Boto3 code.
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to list S3 objects programmatically. (Task) Write Boto3 code to list bucket objects. (Action): import boto3; s3 = boto3.client('s3', region_name='ap-south-1'); response = s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket='my-bucket-name'); for obj in response.get('Contents', []): print(obj['Key']). This uses the S3 client's list_objects_v2 method. The response dict contains a 'Contents' key with a list of object metadata dictionaries. Each dict has a 'Key' (the object name/path). (Result) Script prints all object keys in the bucket. For buckets with more than 1,000 objects, you must handle pagination using the 'NextContinuationToken' in the response.

questions.question: Describe the full architecture of a production static website on AWS — from file storage to a customer visiting with a custom domain name over HTTPS.
questions.answer: (Situation) Build a production-grade static website. (Task) Architect end-to-end using AWS services. (Action) Full architecture: (1) S3 bucket — private, stores all HTML/CSS/JS/image files, static website hosting enabled. (2) OAC — attached to CloudFront distribution, updates S3 bucket policy to allow only CloudFront access. (3) ACM — SSL certificate for the custom domain, created in us-east-1. (4) CloudFront distribution — origin is S3, OAC attached, custom domain attached with ACM certificate, viewer protocol policy set to HTTPS only. (5) Route 53 — hosted zone for the domain, Alias A record pointing to CloudFront distribution. (Result) User visits www.mycompany.com over HTTPS. Route 53 resolves to CloudFront. Nearest edge location serves cached content. If cache miss, CloudFront fetches from private S3. User gets fast, secure content delivery globally.

questions.question: What is the difference between AWS Console, CLI, and SDK — when would you use each in a real-world DevOps role?
questions.answer: All three interact with the same underlying AWS APIs. Console: Web browser GUI. Use for learning, visual exploration, one-off configurations, and troubleshooting. Not automatable. CLI: Terminal tool. Use for scripting, quick automated tasks, shell-based pipelines, and day-to-day operations. Syntax: 'aws s3 ls'. SDK (Boto3): Programming language integration. Use when building applications that need AWS integration, writing complex automation logic, integrating with CI/CD pipelines, or processing large volumes of AWS API calls. In real DevOps roles: Console is rarely used for production tasks. CLI is used for scripts and quick operations. SDK is used for everything that needs to run as part of an application or automated workflow.

questions.question: How does CloudFront's caching behavior work with dynamic vs static content? When should you disable caching?
questions.answer: Static content (images, CSS, JS, HTML) — CloudFront caches these at edge locations for the duration of the TTL. Subsequent requests are served from cache without hitting the origin. Dynamic content (API responses, user-specific data, real-time prices) — by default CloudFront would cache these too, which would serve stale data. Solution: For dynamic content, configure a CloudFront behavior with minimum TTL = 0 and forward all headers/cookies to the origin. This effectively disables caching for those paths. Alternatively, set Cache-Control: no-cache headers in your origin responses. Best practice: Use separate CloudFront behaviors for /api/* (no cache, forward to backend) and /* (cached, served from S3).

questions.question: Explain how Route 53 Latency-based routing works. How is it different from Geolocation routing?
questions.answer: Latency-based routing: Route 53 measures the actual network latency between the user's IP and each configured AWS region. It routes requests to the region with the lowest measured latency — not necessarily the geographically closest region. This is dynamic and can change as network conditions change. Geolocation routing: Routes traffic based on the geographic location of the user (country or continent), regardless of actual latency. A user in Brazil always goes to the same endpoint even if a US server happens to have lower latency that day. Use latency-based for best performance optimization. Use geolocation for data sovereignty requirements (e.g., EU users must stay in EU), content localization (different languages by country), or compliance needs.

questions.question: A large e-commerce company has its product images in S3. They want CloudFront to cache images for 7 days but HTML pages for only 5 minutes. How do they configure this?
questions.answer: This requires multiple CloudFront cache behaviors. In the distribution, create two behaviors: (1) Path pattern /images/* — set minimum TTL 604800 (7 days), maximum TTL 604800, default TTL 604800. Or configure the S3 origin to send Cache-Control: max-age=604800 headers for image objects, and CloudFront will honor them. (2) Path pattern /* (default) — set minimum TTL 300 (5 minutes), maximum TTL 300. Or set Cache-Control: max-age=300 on HTML responses. CloudFront evaluates path patterns in order of specificity and applies the matching behavior's settings. This ensures images are cached aggressively (reducing S3 requests) while HTML stays fresh for near-real-time content updates.

questions.question: What is the Boto3 credential resolution order? Why does IAM role take precedence for EC2 instances?
questions.answer: Boto3 resolves credentials in this order: (1) Explicitly passed credentials in the code (not recommended). (2) Environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN). (3) AWS credentials file (~/.aws/credentials). (4) AWS config file (~/.aws/config). (5) Container credentials (for ECS tasks). (6) EC2 instance profile / IAM role (via instance metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254). For EC2 instances, the IAM role (item 6) is the recommended and most secure approach because: temporary credentials are automatically rotated every hour by AWS STS, no long-lived keys are stored anywhere, and the principle of least privilege is enforced per role policy. No developer intervention is needed to refresh credentials.
